title: Shared task scores carried 87 percent of input-fingerprint prediction gain in 176 mouse regions under spatial validation
abstract: We tested whether input wiring predicts general task decodability or relative task profiles in 176 IBL mouse brain regions. We split five standardized task scores into a common component and an orthogonal profile. Kernel ridge models used nested random and spatial validation with training-only scaling and tuning. On spatial splits, input fingerprints reduced common-component error by 31.6 percent and profile error by 5.4 percent relative to geometry and division. Both gains exceeded zero in each of five partitions. The common component held 53.8 percent of standardized task variance but carried 86.9 percent of input gain when both components used the same total-variance scale. Relative profiles retained a smaller gain beyond types and output fingerprints. Removal of training PC1 gave a similar result. The profile input model reduced error by 7.0 percent against a mean-only predictor. Thus most anatomical prediction gain in these models concerns shared task scores, with some transferable profile information. The data do not separate shared biological engagement from sampling and recording quality. Results depend on summary scores, model choices and overlapping partitions. They do not establish causal wiring control or new spatial-null significance.

display.caption: Input fingerprints improve the common task component more than relative task profiles. Bars show mean error gains; lines show ranges over five overlapping partitions.
The common component carries 80.7 percent of input gain on random splits and 86.9 percent on spatial splits. Points show five partitions, not independent experiments.
